title: "Day 3 — Control Flow + Functions"
subtitle: "Week 1 · if as a value, `case_when`, `...` vs `*args`, guards & closures"

## Cheat sheet (60 seconds)

| Task | R | Python |
|---|---|---|
| conditional value | `x <- if (a) 1 else 2` | `x = 1 if a else 2` |
| vectorized branch | `if_else(cond, a, b)` | `np.where(cond, a, b)` |
| multi-case (row-wise) | `case_when(...)` | `np.select([...], [...])` |
| dispatch on value | `switch(type, A = 1, B = 2)` | `dict` lookup |
| optional args | `f(x, trim = 0)` | `def f(x, trim=0)` |
| any extra args | `f(...)` | `*args, **kwargs` |
| raise error | `stop("msg")` | `raise ValueError("msg")` |
| check inputs | `stopifnot(...)` | `assert` / explicit `if` |
| named guard messages | `stopifnot("msg" = cond)` | `assert cond, "msg"` |

## `if` is a value in R (a superpower)

In R, `if` is not a *statement* — it's an **expression** that returns a
value, like everything else in the language. You can assign it, put it in a
`mutate()`, pass it to a function:

```{webr}
#| label: ifvalue
score <- 87

grade  <- if (score > 90) "A" else "B"     # the if EXPRESSION returns a value
grade

status <- if (score > 90) {
  "A"                    # braces also return their last expression
} else if (score > 80) {
  "B"
} else {
  "C"
}
status
```

In Python the same idea is the ternary:

```python
score = 87
grade = "A" if score > 90 else "B"
```

Where this matters daily: inside `mutate()`, `if_else()` *is* the value-form
of `if` applied to whole columns. Scalar `if` for single decisions,
`if_else`/`case_when` for vectors — never the reverse.

## Vectorized branching: the workhorse

Never loop to branch element-by-element — branch on whole columns:

```{webr}
#| label: casewhen
library(dplyr)

tibble(pvalue = c(1e-12, 0.03, 0.2, 0.7)) |>
  mutate(stars = case_when(
    pvalue < 0.001 ~ "***",
    pvalue < 0.01  ~ "**",
    pvalue < 0.05  ~ "*",
    .default       = "ns"     # catch-all, keeps order explicit
  ))
```

`case_when` is evaluated **top-down, first match wins** — exactly like an
`elif` chain, which is why *ordering is logic*: swapping the first two rows
would break the significance ladder. Unmatched values (and `NA` conditions)
fall through to `.default`; if you skip `.default`, unmatched rows become
`NA` — count them when you test.

```python
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
p = pd.Series([1e-12, 0.03, 0.2, 0.7])
pd.Series(np.select(
    [p < 0.001, p < 0.01, p < 0.05],
    ["***", "**", "*"],
    default="ns"))
```

::: {.callout-warning}
## Subtle difference
R's `case_when` chains conditions top-down per value; `np.select` checks the
**condition lists** in order, same semantics — but in Python remember
conditions apply to the *whole array at once*, in the order given. First match
wins in both.
:::

## Loops: allowed, but know when

```{webr}
#| label: loops
# The classic AI-generated bug:
v <- c()
# for (i in 1:length(v)) print(v[i])   # BUG: 1:0 = c(1,0), loop runs twice!

seq_along(v)   # empty — the loop body never runs. Correct tool.
```

Legit loop uses: **iterative algorithms with memory** (MCMC chains, EM
iterations, Gibbs samplers), `while` until convergence, side-effects across
files. The decision rule:

> Transformation → vectorize / map. Iteration where each step *needs the
> previous step's result* → loop.

```{webr}
#| label: loop-ok
# A legitimate loop: each value needs the previous one
x <- numeric(10); x[1] <- 1
for (i in 2:10) x[i] <- 0.5 * x[i - 1] + 1
round(x, 3)
```

```python
# Python: empty-range loops just don't run — no 1:0 trap
v = []
for i in range(len(v)):   # zero iterations
    print(v[i])

# the same legit loop, pythonic version
import itertools
xs = list(itertools.accumulate(range(10), lambda acc, _: 0.5 * acc + 1, initial=1))[1:]
```

## Functions that don't embarrass you

```{webr}
#| label: function
#' Fold-change with a guard clause
#'
#' @param treat numeric, treated intensities
#' @param ctrl  numeric, control intensities
#' @param pseudo numeric, added to both to avoid divide-by-zero
log2fc <- function(treat, ctrl, pseudo = 1) {
  stopifnot(
    "treat must be numeric" = is.numeric(treat),
    "ctrl must be numeric"  = is.numeric(ctrl),
    "lengths must match"    = length(treat) == length(ctrl)
  )
  log2((treat + pseudo) / (ctrl + pseudo))
}

log2fc(c(32, 8), c(2, 2))
log2fc("oops", 2)   # error message a human can read
```

Anatomy, top to bottom: **roxygen comment → guard clauses → one job →
last expression is the return value.** Guards turn cryptic downstream
failures ("non-numeric argument to binary operator", nine frames deep) into
immediate, named ones at the source — this is 80% of "robust code", and it
costs three lines.

Why name the conditions? Unnamed `stopifnot()` just prints the *call* that
failed — useless for anyone who didn't write it. Named conditions print the
message you wrote.

```python
import numpy as np

def log2fc(treat, ctrl, pseudo=1):
    """Fold-change with a guard clause."""
    treat, ctrl = np.asarray(treat, float), np.asarray(ctrl, float)
    if treat.shape != ctrl.shape:
        raise ValueError("treat and ctrl must have the same shape")
    return np.log2((treat + pseudo) / (ctrl + pseudo))
```

Python's `assert` is *not* the same tool: asserts vanish under `python -O`
(optimized mode). For validation that must always run, use explicit
`raise ValueError(...)`.

## The dots: `...` vs `*args/**kwargs`

```{webr}
#| label: dots
mean_style <- function(x, ...) {
  mean(x, ...)          # ... forwards: na.rm = TRUE lands in mean()
}

mean_style(c(1, NA, 3), na.rm = TRUE)
```

```python
def mean_style(x, *args, **kwargs):
    print(f"extra kwargs: {kwargs}")
    return sum(x) / len(x)

mean_style([1, 2, 3], na_rm=True)
```

Use `...` to **forward arguments to inner functions** — that's its 90% use.
The danger is equal and opposite: typos vanish into `...` silently
(`mean_style(x, narm = TRUE)` just ignores your typo), so keep forwarding
interfaces narrow.

## Scope, closures, and two R quirks

```{webr}
#| label: closure
make_scaler <- function(center) {
  function(x) x - center       # remembers `center` from birth environment
}

scale_to_brca1 <- make_scaler(center = 12.5)
scale_to_brca1(c(10, 12.5, 20))
```

```python
import numpy as np

def make_scaler(center):
    def scale(x):
        return np.asarray(x) - center   # closure over center
    return scale
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## Where you already use closures
`purrr::partial()`, ggplot `aes()` mappings, sklearn `Pipeline` steps,
functools — all ship captured state around in functions. Recognizing closures
makes all of them stop being magic.
:::

**Quirk 1 — lazy defaults.** R default arguments are evaluated *inside* the
function, at use time — so a default can reference other arguments:

```{webr}
#| label: lazy
rescale <- function(x, lo = min(x), hi = max(x)) {
  (x - lo) / (hi - lo)
}
rescale(c(10, 20, 30))     # defaults computed from THIS x
```

```python
# Python evaluates defaults ONCE at definition time — never do this:
def danger(x, bucket=[]):        # the mutable-default bug
    bucket.append(x)
    return bucket
print(danger(1), danger(2))      # [1], [1, 2]  ← shared list!
```

**Quirk 2 — partial matching.** `mean(x = 1:3, na.rm = TRUE)` works, and so
would `mean(1:3, na = TRUE)` — R completes unambiguous prefixes. Convenient
for the console, poisonous for scripts (new argument `na_action` breaks your
`na =` silently). Always write full argument names in code.

## Drills (live pad)

```{webr}
#| label: drills
library(dplyr)

# 1. Assign "sig"/"ns" to p <- 0.049 using if as a value

# 2. case_when: label mtcars$hp into "low" (<100), "mid" (<180), "high"

# 3. Write safe_log(x) that errors clearly if any x <= 0

# 4. switch: given method <- "pearson", return "cor", for "spearman" "cov"

# 5. make_power(n) returning a function that raises x to the n-th power

# 6. Vectorized ternary: mpg above median → "thirsty" else "sippy"

# 7. default-args trick: function geomean(x, logx = log(x)) returning exp(mean(logx))
#    (careful with zeros!)

# 8. A function nth_root(x, n = 2) with a guard for negative x when n is even

# 9. Forwarding dots: my_sum(x, ...) that calls sum(x, ...) — test na.rm on chars

# 10. case_when on a factor: recode mtcars$cyl 4→"four" 6→"six" 8→"eight"

# 11. What does switch("b", a = 1, b = 2, 99) return? predict, then run

# 12. Write is_monotonic(x): TRUE if x is non-decreasing — guard empty vectors
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Expected answers
1. `status <- if (p < 0.05) "sig" else "ns"`
2. `case_when(hp < 100 ~ "low", hp < 180 ~ "mid", .default = "high")`
3. `safe_log <- function(x) { stopifnot("x must be > 0" = all(x > 0)); log(x) }`
4. `switch(method, pearson = "cor", spearman = "cov")`
5. `make_power <- function(n) function(x) x^n`
6. `if_else(mtcars$mpg > median(mtcars$mpg), "thirsty", "sippy")`
7. `geomean <- function(x, logx = log(x)) exp(mean(logx))` — zeros give -Inf; guard or filter
8. `nth_root <- function(x, n = 2) { stopifnot("even root of negative" = !(n %% 2 == 0 && x < 0)); x^(1/n) }`
9. `my_sum <- function(x, ...) sum(x, ...)`
10. `case_match(mtcars$cyl, 4 ~ "four", 6 ~ "six", 8 ~ "eight")`
11. `2` — named dispatch, falls to default only on miss
12. `is_monotonic <- function(x) { if (length(x) < 2) return(TRUE); all(diff(x) >= 0) }`
:::

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 — case_when classifier

Classify expression: `expr < 1` → "silent", `1–5` → "low", `5–20` → "medium",
`> 20` → "high". Order matters — boundaries go the clean way.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-cw
library(dplyr)

genes <- tibble::tibble(gene = c("XIST", "MYC", "GAPDH", "NONE"),
                        expr = c(0.2, 55.0, 4.4, 12.0))

genes |>
  mutate(level = ______)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-cw"}
Strict inequalities chained top-down: `expr < 1 ~ "silent"`, `expr < 5 ~ "low"`,
`expr < 20 ~ "medium"`, `.default = "high"`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-cw"}
```r
genes |>
  mutate(level = case_when(
    expr < 1  ~ "silent",
    expr < 5  ~ "low",
    expr < 20 ~ "medium",
    .default  = "high"
  ))
```
:::

### Exercise 2 — a function with guards

Write `shannon_entropy(probs)` = `-sum(p * log2(p))`. Guards: numeric,
non-negative, sum to 1 (within 0.01). Return the entropy.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-shannon
shannon_entropy <- function(probs) {
  ______
}

shannon_entropy(c(0.5, 0.5))        # 1
shannon_entropy(c(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 0.25))  # 2
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-shannon"}
Guard with `stopifnot()`; then filter out zeros before logging
(`log2(0) = -Inf`): `probs[probs > 0]`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-shannon"}
```r
shannon_entropy <- function(probs) {
  stopifnot(
    "probs must be numeric" = is.numeric(probs),
    "probs must be >= 0"    = all(probs >= 0),
    "probs must sum to 1"   = abs(sum(probs) - 1) < 0.01
  )
  p <- probs[probs > 0]
  -sum(p * log2(p))
}
```
:::

### Exercise 3 — closure factory

Build `make_threshold_labeler(threshold)` that returns a function labeling
values `"above"`/`"below"`. Create one at 0.05 and test on `c(0.01, 0.2)`.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-closure
make_threshold_labeler <- function(threshold) {
  ______
}

label_p <- make_threshold_labeler(0.05)
label_p(c(0.01, 0.2))
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-closure"}
Return an anonymous function that captures `threshold`:
`function(x) if_else(x < threshold, "below", "above")`.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-closure"}
```r
make_threshold_labeler <- function(threshold) {
  function(x) if_else(x < threshold, "below", "above")
}
```
:::

### Exercise 4 — the lazy-default superpower

Write `z_score(x, mu = mean(x), sigma = sd(x))` returning `(x - mu) / sigma`.
The one-liner should work both standardize-itself *and* standardize against
supplied training parameters — the exact pattern sklearn's `StandardScaler`
encodes. (Why `sigma`, not `sd`? Naming an argument `sd` would shadow
`base::sd()` inside its own default — a promise-recursion error. Function
names make bad parameter names.)

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-z
z_score <- function(x, mu = mean(x), sigma = sd(x)) {
  ______
}

z_score(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5))          # self-standardized
z_score(c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5), mu = 0, sigma = 2)  # against training params
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-z"}
Body is just `(x - mu) / sigma` — the laziness does the rest.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-z"}
```r
z_score <- function(x, mu = mean(x), sigma = sd(x)) {
  (x - mu) / sigma
}
```
:::

### Exercise 5 — switchboard

Write `nucleotide_color(base)` returning "A"→"green", "C"→"blue",
"G"→"yellow", "T"→"red" via `switch`, and unknown bases → "grey". Guard:
input must be a single character string.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex-d3-switch
nucleotide_color <- function(base) {
  ______
}

sapply(c("A", "G", "T", "N"), nucleotide_color)
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex-d3-switch"}
`switch(toupper(base), A = "green", C = "blue", G = "yellow", T = "red", "grey")`
— the unnamed last argument is the default.
:::

::: {.solution exercise="ex-d3-switch"}
```r
nucleotide_color <- function(base) {
  stopifnot("base must be a single string" =
              is.character(base) && length(base) == 1)
  switch(toupper(base),
         A = "green", C = "blue",
         G = "yellow", T = "red",
         "grey")
}
```
:::

## Common pitfalls (real ones)

::: {.callout-warning}
## 1. Floating-point `==`
`0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3` is `FALSE` — binary floats. Compare with a tolerance:
`isTRUE(all.equal(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))` (R) or `math.isclose(...)` (Python).
This bug lives in p-value and coordinate comparisons everywhere.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 2. Unnamed `stopifnot()`
`stopifnot(is.numeric(x))` on failure prints `is.numeric(x) is not TRUE` —
true but useless. Always name: `stopifnot("x must be numeric" = is.numeric(x))`.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## 3. `case_when` silent NAs
Forget `.default` and unmatched rows become `NA` with no warning. After any
new `case_when`, `count(df, new_col)` — if an unexpected `NA` appears,
your cases don't cover the data.
:::

## Self-quiz — predict the output

```{webr}
#| label: quiz
# Q1: what prints?
f <- function(a, b = a * 2) a + b
f(3)

# Q2: what prints?
case_when(c(TRUE, FALSE, NA) ~ "y", .default = "n")

# Q3: what prints?
g <- function(...) list(...)$z
g(z = 5, w = 6)

# Q4: what prints — and is this a good idea?
h <- function(x = rnorm(1)) x
c(h(), h())

# Q5: what prints?
k <- function(x) { x <- x * 10; x }
n <- 5
k(n)
n
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Quiz answers
1. `9` — `b` defaults to `a * 2` = 6, then `3 + 6`. Lazy defaults see the
   same arguments.
2. `"y" "n" "n"` — the NA condition falls through to `.default`. Watch for
   this silently changing NA rows!
3. `5` — `...` collects named args; you can pick them out by name
4. Two *different* random numbers — each call re-evaluates the default.
   (Good for rnorm, terrible for `bucket = list()` — Python evaluates once!)
5. `50` then `5` — R passes by value; the function got a copy.
   (pandas DataFrames are the opposite — mutate-in-place traps live there.)
:::

## Wrap-up checklist

- [ ] `if` returns a value; `case_when` is my vectorized elif
- [ ] `seq_along()` not `1:length(x)` — always
- [ ] Every function I write has guards (`stopifnot`) for anything a human could fat-finger
- [ ] `...` forwards args; closures capture state; lazy defaults reference arguments
- [ ] I scored 5/5 on the self-quiz
